dossier.public_summary: The 14.3-day dip is not a regular planet transit. Odd and even events have very different depths, and a second eclipse is seen near phase 0.5 that mimics a stellar companion's orbit. The transits also vary by sector and the 14-day period is twice the star's 7-day spin. Together this points to an eclipsing binary with variable eclipses on the M-dwarf target.

reasons.why: Odd and even transits differ strongly (depth_odd 4336 ppm vs depth_even 1681 ppm, ratio 2.6, difference 2655 ppm, 61% ) with red_noise 1.023 indicating coherent alternate-depth signal, best explained by an eclipsing binary at twice the 14.3 d period.

A secondary dip at phase 0.4705 (0.02945 offset from 0.5) with depth 1216 ppm and depth_over_dip 0.4324, snr 4.772 vs best_brightening_snr 3.714, indicates a second eclipse consistent with a stellar companion.
Individual transits are inconsistent (chi2 29.33 dof 3, 4 transits, share_of_top_3 0.991) pointing to depth variations, not a steady planetary transit.

Signal period 14.3199 d is 1.98x the rotation period (7.2195 d), detected in sector 56 with amplitude 4759 ppm, while flat-bottom shape (v_sigma -3.515, duration ratio 1.101) is also produced by total stellar eclipses, so the coincidence cannot favor a planet over an EB.
Planet-rank 0.1 is in the bottom decile of known planets, consistent with the low true-planet rate for this combination of odd/even and secondary and depth instability.
